rows.evidence: Q1: Section 5 (Tables 2-6, Figs 4-7) reports the authors' own benchmark measurements of program size, memory, processing time, transaction cost/time on Ropsten, and energy consumption of six microcontroller boards running their water-metering-to-blockchain library.
rows.notes: The study builds a proof-of-concept in which a YF-201 flow sensor on a constrained device signs and sends water-consumption transactions to Ethereum, and measures only device-level overheads (energy, memory, time) and transaction costs/latency. Trust, data security and facilitation of water sharing among farmers are asserted by design (cryptographic signing, permissionless ledger) in Section 3, not measured or tested with any users, farmers or stakeholders. The study therefore shows only a technical precondition (constrained devices can act as direct blockchain data sources) for the claimed social effect.

rows.evidence: Q1: Section 5 (Tables 2-6, Figs 4-7) reports the authors' own measurements of device footprints, processing time, blockchain transaction cost and latency, and energy budget for the metering-to-blockchain proof-of-concept.
rows.notes: No water-use, water-saving or water-use-efficiency outcome is measured. The reward smart contract (Reward() relative to a threshold) is implemented but its effect on farmer water consumption is never tested; irrigation schedules are only assumed (2 h twice a day) to compute the device energy budget. The study shows a technical feasibility precondition (metering devices can report consumption directly to a public blockchain at ~6% extra energy) rather than any effect on water-use efficiency.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is an engineering proof-of-concept evaluating IoT-device overheads of blockchain integration; it contains no field trial, survey or observational data on trust among farmers or on water consumption outcomes, so both claim rows rest on asserted rather than demonstrated effects.
